title: The Promise and Peril of AI Legal Services to Equalize Justice
pub: Harvard Journal on Law & Technology (JOLT) Digest
author: Ashwin Telang

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Cheaper assistance: More participation may not yield remedies
st.an: The source presents digitized legal services as a possible response to the justice gap and acknowledges that legal complexity complicates automation, but it provides no empirical evidence and does not address the cluster’s core distinction between increased participation and effective remedies.
qs: **Background**  The digitization of legal services could ameliorate America's problem with access to justice.
Law is a complex and dynamic field, complicating the task of those seeking to automate it.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts selective, human-centred deployment: AI can supplement lawyers and expand access through routine assistance, but unequal access, bias and low-quality services can worsen injustice. It materially extends the cluster by proposing transparency, competition policy and supervised regulatory sandboxes to preserve quality and distribute benefits more equitably.
qs: As legal technology gathers momentum, an approach of “technology is better than nothing” will not suffice.
Regulators must act soon to contain negative spillovers from legal technology to ensure it can shrink the justice gap, not enlarge it.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: Telang strongly supports the cluster’s balanced proposition: legal AI can expand affordable assistance, but unequal access, bias and weak quality controls could shift risk onto low-income users and institutionalize inferior service. He also aligns with its rejection of an unqualified “better than nothing” standard and its preference for regulation and supervised experimentation.
qs: If legal technology is the only affordable service available to impoverished Americans, this vulnerable population will be at the whim of those who control the technology; service providers could, predictably, overlook low-income sectors, disregarding the quality of legal service.
As legal technology gathers momentum, an approach of “technology is better than nothing” will not suffice.

st.t: Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
st.an: Telang supports the cluster’s central proposition that AI may lower barriers to civil legal assistance while creating risks that require protection and accountability. His reported chatbot and software successes are illustrative rather than systematic evidence, and his general call for regulation does not develop a specific reform framework.
qs: As Congress fails to act to protect the rights of underserved Americans, legal technologies can ameliorate the issue, transforming and expanding access to justice.
Still in an experimental and developmental phase, this technology must be steered and regulated to minimize future negative outcomes.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Telang aligns with the synthesis’s cautious, supervised framing: legal AI can automate or assist bounded tasks while supplementing rather than replacing lawyers’ core capabilities. He also treats access-to-justice gains as contingent and potentially unequal, concluding that still-experimental systems require active steering and regulation. The source does not materially address verification or apprenticeship risks, so it supports rather than extends the full synthesis.
qs: Susskind argues automation will never replace a lawyer’s strategy, logic, creativity, and empathy — machine learning can only supplement them.
Still in an experimental and developmental phase, this technology must be steered and regulated to minimize future negative outcomes.

kp.d: Telang argues that emerging AI can perform some lawyer functions, simplify complex law and reduce the cost barriers that contribute to the civil justice gap. The article frames this as potential rather than an established outcome and conditions it on appropriate design and regulation.
qs: However, new developments in artificial intelligence (“AI”) promise to fulfill many functions of a lawyer and democratize the law.
The digitization of legal services could ameliorate America's problem with access to justice.
Artificial intelligence shows promise for equalizing access to justice, but it also presents perils of exacerbating inequalities.

kp.k: Civil legal needs remain overwhelmingly unmet
kp.d: As background evidence for the need for lower-cost services, the article reports that nearly 92% of impoverished Americans—36 million people—cannot afford counsel in civil suits, affecting matters such as eviction, healthcare and domestic abuse, with disproportionate consequences for women and people of color.
qs: Nearly 92% of impoverished Americans, or 36 million people, cannot afford to hire a lawyer for a civil suit.
This “judicial deficit” perpetuates poverty and compromises the fundamental rights lawyers are meant to protect, affecting issues spanning from eviction to healthcare to domestic abuse.
Making matters worse, injustices from these lawyerless courts disproportionately affect women and people of color.

kp.k: Legal technology investment and development are expanding
kp.d: The article characterizes legal AI as experimental but cites market activity as evidence of momentum: more than 280 companies, over $757 million raised and 1,369 legal machine-learning patent filings. It does not provide the underlying study period or methodology for these figures.
qs: Even at this experimental stage, over 280 companies have started developing legal technology.
Companies in this space have already raised over $757 million and filed for 1,369 legal machine-learning patents.

kp.d: The source reports that automated systems can rapidly file, organize and generate legal documents. It presents Intelligent File 1.0 and Rocket Lawyer as examples of tools handling paperwork and reducing doctrinal and procedural barriers for people acting without lawyers.
qs: Automated legal systems have the capability to handle legal files in a matter of seconds.
A recent AI system, Intelligent File 1.0, can automatically file and organize legal documents.
Apps such as Rocket Lawyer are already helping impoverished Americans by instantly completing legal paperwork, such as business contracts, real estate agreements, and wills.

The technology behind these systems simplifies complex legal doctrines and formalities, mitigating structural barriers to understanding the law without a lawyer and completing even the simplest legal tasks.

kp.k: Chatbots may provide low-cost legal guidance
kp.d: The article argues that self-help chatbots can supply immediate, situation-specific information about rights, strategy and civil procedure. It cites rAInbow as a machine-learning application intended to identify legal protections for potential domestic-violence victims and explain legal terminology.
qs: Beyond simplifying documentation, AI can also answer legal questions and offer assistance at low costs.
Self-help chatbots empower low-income individuals to take their civil issues to court by providing immediate legal information about their specific case or situation.
These chatbots are designed to advise clients about their rights, legal strategies, and procedures in civil court.
A new chatbot app, rAInbow, can also identify areas of legal protection for potential victims of domestic violence.

kp.k: Reported examples suggest substantial task capability
kp.d: The article reports that Do Not Pay overturned more than 100,000 speeding tickets and saved low-income Americans millions of dollars. It also relays bankruptcy lawyer Luis Salazar’s assessment that software quickly produced a simple two-page memo and analyzed a complex legal problem similarly to a human lawyer; these are reported examples rather than independently evaluated findings in the article.
qs: The website Do Not Pay overturned over 100,000 speeding tickets, saving low-income Americans millions of dollars.
Luis Salazar, a bankruptcy lawyer, tested new legal software against his own skills, and the results, he said, “blew me away.”
A machine could quickly produce a simple two-page memo and analyze a complex legal problem very similar to what a human lawyer could produce.

kp.k: Automation may supplement rather than replace lawyers
kp.d: The article attributes to Richard Susskind a copilot-style account of legal technology: machines can accelerate mundane work and free lawyers for more difficult and creative tasks, but cannot replace human strategy, logic, creativity and empathy. This is Susskind’s reported position, not an empirical finding established by the article.
qs: Richard Susskind, a lawyer, rebuts these concerns, arguing that lawyers and technology can work alongside each other.
Legal technology can help law firms by speeding up mundane, time-consuming tasks and allowing lawyers to focus on more challenging, creative endeavors.
Susskind argues automation will never replace a lawyer’s strategy, logic, creativity, and empathy — machine learning can only supplement them.

kp.k: Legal AI could create two-tiered justice
kp.d: Telang’s central warning is that unregulated AI could widen rather than close the justice gap. The article identifies three mechanisms: premium systems may be limited to large firms, disadvantaged communities may lack access to any system, and policymakers may treat inferior digital tools as a substitute for a right to human civil counsel.
qs: Drew Simshaw, an assistant professor at the Gonzaga University School of Law, writes that legal AI could create an inequitable “two-tiered system.”
First, high-quality AI may be expensive and thus only available to larger law firms, presenting a power asymmetry between law firms and individuals.
Second, many impoverished Americans and people of color may be unable to access any AI in the first place.
Third, the advent of legal AI may lead Congress to believe that impoverished individuals no longer need human civil lawyers, thereby halting movement on a long-requested right to civil counsel.

kp.k: AI adoption may widen law-firm disparities
kp.d: The article predicts a reinforcing competitive cycle in which large firms can fund high-quality AI, experiment safely, automate administrative work and expand geographically, while smaller firms lack equivalent capital and organizational resources. It argues that this provider-side disparity would disadvantage lower- and middle-income clients whose lawyers face technology-enabled wealthy firms.
qs: Unregulated legal AI locks law firms into a mutually reinforcing cycle that only makes rich firms richer and widens revenue gaps between firms.

Larger law firms are often better equipped to adopt emerging legal technologies; advanced AI is costly to obtain and adopt, and is thus only available to wealthy firms who have the necessary capital and funding capacity to pursue it.
By automating administrative tasks, national firms can also expand in size and geography.
Individual lawyers representing lower- to middle-income Americans face a disadvantage against wealthy firms able to take advantage of AI technology and the superior work it can help produce.

kp.k: Digital exclusion limits access to legal AI
kp.d: The article cites unreliable internet service, inadequate broadband and limited technological skills as practical barriers, especially across age, race, geography, education and income. It reports that one in five Americans lacks reliable internet access and warns that such gaps could exclude vulnerable communities from both AI tools and justice systems.
qs: Accessibility gaps in communications technology loom large, especially in line with age, race, geography, education, and income gaps.
By one measure, one in five Americans do not have reliable internet access.
There is also a technological gap — many would-be pro se litigants lack the “necessary skills and resources to make meaningful use of technologies.”
These technology gaps could functionally shut many vulnerable communities out of legal AI and justice systems.

kp.k: Standardized systems may exclude diverse users
kp.d: Telang argues that access-to-justice tools must support multiple languages, cultural communication styles, storytelling structures and nonverbal or nonwritten inputs. One-size-fits-all information gathering may misunderstand users who do not communicate through free-flowing, chronological narratives.
qs: Broadly, “self-help” legal services must transcend a one-size-fits-all model.

For one, most digital legal services are not multilingual or otherwise do not offer services in many languages — an especially concerning exclusion given that non-English speakers are a significant chunk of lawyerless litigants.
Sherley Cruz also highlights the importance of “accounting for different cultures’ communication styles.”
Likewise, current AI legal services do not appear to account for non-chronological storytelling and different forms of communication inputs beyond verbal/written forms existing in other cultures.

kp.k: Biased training data can automate inequality
kp.d: The article reports that chatbots trained on sources including scraped language and Reddit can produce racist and biased responses. It attributes to Amy Cyphert the view that systems reinforcing stereotypes should not be used and argues that automating these biases makes current tools unfit to close the justice gap.
qs: Using datasets from sources including scraped language and Reddit, AI chatbots that provide legal advice can sometimes produce overtly racist and biased responses.

Amy Cyphert argues that these AI technologies produce these results specifically because they are trained this way and “should not be used” to the extent that they reinforce biased stereotypes and further marginalize users.
In not only reproducing but also automating inequalities, these algorithmic biases simply are not fit to close the justice gap.

kp.k: Cheap AI may displace human-centered reforms
kp.d: The article predicts that if AI becomes the only affordable option for poor litigants, providers may neglect service quality and normalize a subordinate tier of justice. It further speculates that policymakers may abandon campaigns for publicly funded civil counsel in favor of cheaper but inferior digital alternatives.
qs: If legal technology is the only affordable service available to impoverished Americans, this vulnerable population will be at the whim of those who control the technology; service providers could, predictably, overlook low-income sectors, disregarding the quality of legal service.
Without quick intervention, America could soon normalize a lower-tier of justice in the form of low-quality artificial intelligence, wasting the technology’s equalizing potential.
Policymakers will likely abandon human-focused solutions, preferring a cheaper but subordinate digital solution.
All hopes for future human-centered policy solutions would dissipate, dissolving into illusory but inferior legal technologies.

kp.k: Transparency could improve quality and accountability
kp.d: Telang recommends transparency to connect lawyers and technologists, give smaller firms input into system development and expose black-box bias to external review. The article also proposes reporting accuracy rates and certification mechanisms so users and observers can assess service quality.
qs: Regulators can embrace three main avenues to establish effective policies: transparency, competition, and regulatory sandboxes.
Lawyers can help effect meaningful changes in legal technology, such as integrating bias training, cultural consciousness, and other helpful features for clients.
Public transparency could also break through the AI “black box” which makes bias harder to detect.
Reporting accuracy rates of AI, for example, allows onlookers to verify the quality of legal services.
Susan Fortney calls for certifications as a system to check artificial intelligence.

kp.k: Competition could constrain legal AI monopolies
kp.d: The article predicts possible consolidation and recommends policies that preserve competition. It argues that competitive pressure can function as a check on providers by encouraging better algorithms, lower prices, reduced bias and more effective services.
qs: Competition may counter the predicted consolidation of AI legal services in the near future.
Regulatory policies, in response, must aim to boost competition and shut down legal AI monopolies.
Competition is especially essential to push AI developers to improve their algorithms, make their services affordable, remove bias, and provide the most effective legal services.
Here, competition functionally serves as another “check” on AI companies.

kp.k: Ownership restrictions may disadvantage smaller firms
kp.d: The article argues that rules allowing lawyers to invest in technology while barring technology companies from investing in legal practices create asymmetric access to capital. It recommends relaxing ownership and investment restrictions so smaller firms can form relationships with technology providers and adopt AI.
qs: In most American jurisdictions, lawyers can invest in technology, but technology companies can not invest in legal practices.
This creates an asymmetric dynamic wherein wealthier firms have the capital to invest in technology, but smaller firms can not.
Lifting these investment laws could help smaller firms attract the interest of digital AI service providers.
Current law prevents cross-industry relationships between smaller law firms and technologists, thereby cutting off an avenue for smaller firms to adopt new AI.

kp.k: Regulatory sandboxes could broaden affordable services
kp.d: Telang presents closely supervised regulatory sandboxes as a means of testing relaxed ownership and practice restrictions. The article cites Utah’s 2020 legal-services sandbox as the first such initiative and characterizes it as successful in making civil services widely affordable, while recommending expansion to other states.
qs: The best way to do this could be with a regulatory sandbox — an experimental area where certain restrictions are lifted but under close observation of an oversight body.
Ryan Nabil finds that regulatory sandboxes can significantly increase the accessibility of digital justice tools.
In 2020, Utah launched the first regulatory sandbox for legal services, and it was incredibly successful, making civil legal services widely affordable.

Expanding similar regulatory sandboxes to other states can simultaneously expand access to AI legal services for impoverished Americans and smaller law firms, helping them overcome previous financial barriers.

kp.d: The article concludes that accepting AI merely because it is better than no assistance is inadequate. It recommends prompt regulatory intervention, careful calibration and redesign to ensure AI reduces rather than amplifies barriers to justice.
qs: To promote competition and calibration, regulatory innovation must parallel technological innovation.
As legal technology gathers momentum, an approach of “technology is better than nothing” will not suffice.
Regulators must act soon to contain negative spillovers from legal technology to ensure it can shrink the justice gap, not enlarge it.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Telang claims that document automation and low-cost legal chatbots can lower barriers to legal help and expand access to justice.
pts.d: The author describes systems that organize files, complete legal paperwork, explain rights and procedures, and assist with legal analysis. He presents these capabilities as both existing applications and a basis for predicting broader access to justice, particularly for people unable to afford counsel. His examples include Intelligent File 1.0, Rocket Lawyer, rAInbow, and Do Not Pay.

pts.k: Telang presents augmentation as an alternative to lawyer displacement: automation can free lawyers for more demanding work.
pts.d: The author reports displacement concerns but presents an augmentation argument through his discussion of Richard Susskind. The categorical proposition that automation will never replace lawyers' strategy, logic, creativity, and empathy is an argument Telang reports, not an empirical finding established by the article.

pts.k: Telang predicts that unequal capacity to acquire and adopt AI can strengthen wealthy firms, widen firm revenue gaps, and disadvantage less affluent clients.
pts.d: The proposed mechanism is cumulative advantage: large firms can afford advanced systems, absorb experimentation costs, improve both administrative and analytical work, and expand geographically. Smaller firms lack comparable capital and organizational resources and may adopt cheaper tools later. Telang predicts that these provider-side disparities will carry over into unequal quality of representation.

pts.k: Telang claims that digital exclusion and culturally unsuitable or biased systems can prevent legal AI from serving marginalized users.
pts.d: He identifies unreliable internet, inadequate broadband, limited technical skills, insufficient multilingual support, and input formats that fail to accommodate different communication styles. He also claims that training data can generate racist or biased legal-chatbot responses, reproducing and automating inequality rather than closing the justice gap.

pts.k: Telang predicts that inferior AI could become a normalized lower tier of justice and weaken political support for publicly provided human civil counsel.
pts.d: This is a substitution scenario for underserved users: affordable digital assistance could displace the pursuit of human representation even when its quality is inadequate. Telang argues that policymakers may treat AI's availability as evidence that poor litigants no longer need civil lawyers. The article offers a prospective political mechanism rather than a documented instance of Congress abandoning a proposal because of AI.

pts.k: Telang argues that transparency and competition can improve AI quality, affordability, accountability, and suitability for smaller firms.
pts.d: He proposes greater lawyer-technologist collaboration, external review, accuracy reporting, and certification to expose bias and distinguish service quality. He predicts that competition and action against monopolies will encourage better and more affordable products. These are proposed regulatory effects, not evaluated interventions in the article.

pts.k: Telang predicts that relaxing ownership and investment restrictions through supervised regulatory sandboxes can broaden access to legal AI.
pts.d: The author argues that restrictions on technology-company investment in legal practices leave smaller firms without a route to financing AI adoption. He proposes closely supervised experimentation with relaxed restrictions to support cross-industry relationships and expand affordable services. The article discusses these restrictions generally rather than specifying an ABA Model Rule or a particular state's rule text.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The access-expansion claim rests on named applications, reported outcomes, an individual lawyer's experience, and market-development figures.
pts.d: Telang reports that more than 280 companies were developing legal technology, with over $757 million raised and 1,369 legal machine-learning patents filed. He reports a Do Not Pay ticket-overturning outcome and recounts bankruptcy lawyer Luis Salazar's favorable experience with software producing a memo and analyzing a legal problem. These are presented as examples and reported experience, not as standardized comparative tests. The article also supplies an unmet-need statistic as context rather than evidence of AI's effectiveness.

pts.k: The augmentation-versus-displacement discussion relies on a reported expert argument, not employment or task-displacement data.
pts.d: Telang invokes Susskind's authority to support working alongside technology. He supplies no workforce study, employment forecast, or longitudinal evidence establishing that substitution will not occur.

pts.k: The firm-concentration prediction is supported by a resource-based causal argument and cited warnings, rather than measured changes in market concentration.
pts.d: Telang reasons from differences in capital, implementation capacity, and tolerance for trial and error. He also reports expert warnings about two-tier justice and inequality in discrimination litigation. The text supplies no firm-level adoption costs, revenue comparisons, or concentration estimates demonstrating this mechanism.

pts.k: The exclusion and bias claims rely on a connectivity statistic, descriptions of product limitations, and cited scholarly arguments.
pts.d: Telang reports that one in five Americans lacks reliable internet and draws on discussions by Drew Simshaw concerning broadband and skills, Sherley Cruz concerning cultural communication, Amy Cyphert concerning training-related bias, and Cathy O'Neil and Peter Yu concerning algorithmic disadvantage. The article provides no named legal-chatbot bias test, measured incidence of discriminatory output, or quantified legal outcomes for excluded users.

pts.k: The reform claims rely on institutional reasoning, cited authorities, and Telang's favorable account of Utah's sandbox.
pts.d: Telang cites Susan Fortney's certification proposal, calls from legal scholars including Justice Gorsuch to relax investment restrictions, and Ryan Nabil's finding concerning sandbox accessibility. He describes Utah's 2020 launch as successful in making civil legal services affordable, but supplies no outcome figures or AI-specific evaluation establishing the effects of that sandbox.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article distinguishes applications described as already operating in March 2023 from prospective, conditional equalization of justice.
pts.d: Telang calls the technology experimental, while describing some document and chatbot services as available already. The larger claim that AI can transform access to justice has no dated forecast and is qualified by the need to address unequal access, bias, service quality, and regulation. The page's 2026 capture date is not the date of these claims.

pts.k: The concentration scenario concerns current adoption inequalities developing into longer-term advantages, especially without regulation.
pts.d: As of the article's 2023 publication, Telang describes high-quality AI's expense as a present barrier and projects later vulnerability for small firms. He predicts consolidation in the 'near future' but supplies no calendar date. The scenario is explicitly tied to unregulated development and unequal resources.

pts.k: The two-tier and policy-crowding-out predictions are undated near-term warnings conditioned on inadequate intervention and growing reliance on AI.
pts.d: Telang uses 'soon' and 'likely' rather than a dated forecast. The conditions include AI becoming the only affordable service, inadequate provider attention to low-income users, and policymakers accepting deficient digital alternatives as substitutes for human assistance.

pts.k: The regulatory benefits are prospective and depend on prompt, supervised reform alongside technological development.
pts.d: The historical reference is Utah's 2020 sandbox; extending comparable arrangements to other states is a proposal made in 2023. Telang sets no implementation deadline but emphasizes urgency, oversight, and simultaneous regulatory innovation.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The intended beneficiaries are low-income civil litigants and people needing accessible explanations or simple legal documents.
pts.d: Telang emphasizes people confronting eviction, corporate abuses, custody disputes, and domestic violence, as well as users seeking contracts, real estate agreements, or wills. He identifies women and people of color as disproportionately affected by existing failures of access to justice. The envisioned benefit is access to usable legal assistance, not merely enterprise cost savings.

pts.k: Digital and design barriers particularly threaten poor users, people of color, non-English speakers, and would-be self-represented litigants.
pts.d: The author also identifies variation by age, geography, education, and income. Harm can arise from complete exclusion, difficulty communicating legally relevant information, biased responses, or reliance on poor-quality services that are the only affordable option.

pts.k: The proposed reforms target low-income service users, small law firms, AI developers, and legal regulators.
pts.d: Low-income users would gain safeguards against inadequate service and potentially more affordable assistance. Smaller firms would gain input into product design and access to investment and technology. Developers would face external scrutiny and competitive incentives, while regulators would supervise experiments and quality mechanisms.
